name: Geranium

project_scope.selection_mode: two distinct approved Master Plant Pool species; genus lesson only
project_scope.installer_dependency: Neither source-pool species appears in the checked canonical manifest; Approved Taxa Installer owns species-card creation.
project_scope.range_note: No native-range statuses changed or inferred from lesson admission.

look_here_first: Find a complete flowering or fruiting shoot. Both species have palmately cleft leaves and beaked five-part fruits. To separate them, inspect pedicel hairs under magnification: G. texanum has short, backward-pointing hairs pressed flat to the pedicel; G. carolinianum usually has spreading hairs, often including stalked glandular hairs. Confirm with the hair density on the ripe mericarp and flower/fruit dimensions.
shared_genus_traits: Herbaceous, usually annual plants with stipules and simple leaves divided palmately into several lobed segments; leaves may be alternate below and opposite near flowering branches.
Regular flowers with five sepals, five free petals, and ten fertile stamens (unlike Erodium, with five fertile stamens plus five staminodes).
Elongated beaked schizocarp with five one-seeded mericarps that separate from a central column; fruiting structures are more reliable than petal color.

species_comparison_matrix.Geranium carolinianum: Hairs mostly spreading (patent), often a mixture of gland-tipped and non-glandular hairs; backward-directed hairs can occur but are not pressed flat.
species_comparison_matrix.Geranium texanum: Short, non-glandular hairs directed backward (retrorse) and appressed to the pedicel; long-stalked glands lacking.
species_comparison_matrix.how_to_see: Macro both sides of several flower stalks against a dark background; arrows show hair direction relative to flower; record presence/absence of stalked glands.

species_comparison_matrix.character: Mature mericarp hair density (PRIMARY fruit confirmation)
species_comparison_matrix.Geranium carolinianum: Mericarp bodies densely clothed in relatively long hairs.
species_comparison_matrix.Geranium texanum: Mericarp bodies sparsely covered with short hairs.
species_comparison_matrix.how_to_see: Same-scale side view of mature dry fruit body before the mericarps spring away; annotate hair length/density, not just the beak.

species_comparison_matrix.Geranium carolinianum: Usually about 15–19 mm in regional revision.
species_comparison_matrix.how_to_see: Measure intact mature fruit beak with millimeter scale; ranges depend on maturity, so pair with hair characters.

species_comparison_matrix.Geranium texanum: About 4–5 mm in Jepson treatment; small overlap.
species_comparison_matrix.how_to_see: Side-on open flower and ruler; use dimensions only as support, never alone.

species_comparison_matrix.character: Leaf outline (GENUS RECOGNITION, NOT A RELIABLE SPECIES SPLIT)
species_comparison_matrix.Geranium carolinianum: Simple, palmately cleft, usually 5 (sometimes 7) deeply subdivided segments.
species_comparison_matrix.Geranium texanum: Simple, palmately cleft, generally 5–7 deeply subdivided segments.
species_comparison_matrix.how_to_see: Photograph intact mature leaf with central petiole attachment and radiating major veins; teach lobes versus distinct leaflets.

decision_sequence: Confirm Geranium: simple palmately cleft leaves plus five-part beaked fruit; count ten fertile stamens on a suitable flower.
Inspect multiple pedicels at 10×: short appressed retrorse hairs → G. texanum; spreading, often gland-tipped hairs → G. carolinianum.
Check mature mericarp bodies: sparse short hairs favor G. texanum; dense long hairs favor G. carolinianum.
Measure fruit rostrum and petals as supporting characters. If reproductive hairs cannot be inspected, retain Geranium sp. rather than deciding from leaf shape or color.
overlap_cautions: Both have deeply palmate leaves, small pale flowers, and long-beaked fruits. Neither leaf shape nor pink/white flower color is a dependable species split.
G. carolinianum may have few glandular hairs and occasionally backward-directed hairs; their spreading/not-appressed posture remains the key contrast with G. texanum.
Fruit beak length and petal dimensions overlap with developmental stage and treatment; confirm with pedicel and mericarp indumentum.
Older family lesson has a video-fed Erodium reference with unresolved leaf interpretation; do not reuse that image as evidence for Geranium.
Taxa are approved for learner admission by source pool, but neither is canonical here; no new county nativity claim is made.

local_source_pool_lookalikes.separate: A lobed Erodium leaf can resemble Geranium. Count five fertile stamens plus five staminodes in Erodium versus ten fertile stamens in Geranium; fruit separation/awns provide additional context.
E. cicutarium typically has pinnately compound leaves with many divided leaflets, versus Geranium's palmately cleft single blade; verify stamen count.
Do not call a species from a generic long-beaked fruit; photograph pedicel hairs and ripe mericarp bodies.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.character: pedicel hair direction and glandular hairs
diagnostic_photo_checklist.shot: Matched 10× or greater side-on macros of pedicels, labeled flowerward versus stemward, appressed versus spreading hairs, gland heads.
Same-scale mature fruit-body macros before dehiscence; annotate sparse short versus dense long hairs.
Whole intact mature beak with millimeter scale, base and tip both visible.
Measured flower face/side and flower-center macro showing ten anther-bearing stamens.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.character: palmate leaves versus Erodium pinnate leaflets
diagnostic_photo_checklist.shot: Matched intact mature leaves with petiole and annotations for palmate lobes versus rachis/leaflets; comparison species as labeled reference only.

handoffs.question: Both source-pool species absent from manifest; install only after taxonomy identity check, preserve range statuses.
Prioritize matched pedicel hairs and mature mericarps; leaf/flower glamour shots alone do not establish species ID.
